source.author: ov
source.text: Conveniunt illuc popularia flumina primum, nescia, gratentur consolenturne parentem, populifer Sperchios et irrequietus Enipeus Apidanusque senex lenisque Amphrysos et Aeas, moxque amnes alii, qui, qua tulit impetus illos, in mare deducunt fessas erroribus undas.
source.text_original: Conveniunt illuc popularia flumina primum, / nescia, gratentur consolenturne parentem, / populifer Sperchios et irrequietus Enipeus / Apidanusque senex lenisque Amphrysos et Aeas, / moxque amnes alii, qui, qua tulit impetus illos, / in mare deducunt fessas erroribus undas.
source.text_english: There first come together the rivers of the people, unsure whether to rejoice or comfort their parent: the river-teeming Spercheios, restless Enipeus, old Apidanus and gentle Amphrysos and Aias, and soon other streams too, which, wherever their current has borne them, lead their weary waters, worn out by wandering, down into the sea.

reuse.author: val
reuse.text: hinc laevom Telamon pelagus tenet, altior inde occupat Alcides aliud mare, cetera pubes dividitur: celer Asterion, quem matre cadentem Piresius gemino fovit pater amne Cometes, segnior Apidani vires ubi sentit Enipeus.
reuse.text_original: hinc laevom Telamon pelagus tenet, altior inde / occupat Alcides aliud mare, cetera pubes / dividitur: celer Asterion, quem matre cadentem / Piresius gemino fovit pater amne Cometes, / segnior Apidani vires ubi sentit Enipeus.
reuse.text_english: From here Telamon holds the sea to the left; from there Alcides occupies the other sea from a higher place. The rest of the young men are divided: swift Asterion, whom Piresius, his father, as he was falling, nourished with twin rivers, and slower Enipeus, where he feels the strength of the Apidanus.
